text: Warp image pipeline: open with PIL, check mode, cast NumPy to {{c1::float32}}, upload with {{c2::wp.array}}, zero the output, launch the kernel, pull back with {{c3::.numpy()}}, then Image.fromarray and save.
extra: NumPy sits in the middle both ways: PIL to NumPy to Warp, then Warp to NumPy to PIL.

text: Check image.mode first. Mode L is greyscale with NumPy shape {{c1::(h, w)}}. RGB is {{c2::(h, w, 3)}}. RGBA is {{c3::(h, w, 4)}}.
extra: Each channel is one 8-bit unsigned integer per pixel.

text: Pillow image.size is {{c1::(w, h)}}, but a colour NumPy array is {{c2::(h, w, c)}}. Expand greyscale to {{c3::(h, w, 1)}} so one 3D kernel can handle every mode, then strip that axis before you save mode L.
extra: PIL will not build a greyscale image from shape (h, w, 1). Launch with dim equal to the 3D array shape.

text: On RGBA, only filter channels where {{c1::k < 3}} and {{c2::copy alpha unchanged}}. Leave alpha at zero from wp.zeros and you save a {{c3::fully transparent}} image.
extra: Filtering alpha is meaningless. On a fully opaque image the bug still looks fine, so you may not catch it by eye.

text: Set the Warp device to {{c1::"cpu"}} for Docker on a laptop. Use {{c2::"cuda"}} on an Nvidia GPU or Colab.
extra: cpu is the portable serial fallback. cuda runs the kernel in parallel on the GPU.

text: Upload with {{c1::wp.array}}(npInData, dtype=wp.float32, device=device). Allocate the output with {{c2::\(\text{wp.zeros\_like}\)}}(inWarpImage) so it matches shape, dtype, and device, filled with zeros.
extra: On cuda, wp.array copies host memory onto the device. The study guide also allows wp.zeros with an explicit shape.

text: Pass neighbourhood size, unsharp k, or Gaussian sigma into a Warp kernel as {{c1::typed arguments}}. Warp reads each value at {{c2::launch}}, so you can change it without recompiling.
extra: Annotate the type in the signature, then pass the number in inputs=. Closures are for compile-time constants and are not needed in this course.
